text: Compulsory licensing allows the government to authorize use of a patented invention without the patent holder's consent, subject to payment of adequate remuneration. Under the Patents Act 1970, Sections 82-94 govern compulsory licensing. Grounds: patent not worked in India, public not satisfied, patented invention not available at reasonable price, not worked in territory of India. Famous case: Natco Pharma vs Bayer (2012) — first compulsory license granted in India for cancer drug Sorafenib. For AYUSH patents: compulsory licensing can be triggered if patented formulation not manufactured/available in India at reasonable prices.

Section 84 conditions for compulsory license application (after 3 years from grant): 1) Reasonable requirements of public not satisfied. 2) Patented invention not available to public at reasonably affordable price. 3) Patented invention not worked in territory of India. Any 'interested person' can apply to the Controller. Controller considers: nature of invention, time elapsed since grant, measures taken by patentee to work the invention, ability of applicant to work to public advantage. For AYUSH: if a patented formulation is not manufactured in India or priced too high, compulsory license may be granted.

Section 100 allows government use of patented inventions for 'purposes of Government' — broader than compulsory licensing. No application required; government can authorize any person to make, use, sell patented invention. Compensation determined by High Court if parties don't agree. 'Purposes of Government' includes: government hospitals, public health programs, defense, government research. For AYUSH: government can authorize manufacture of patented Ayurvedic medicines for public health programs (e.g., AYUSH dispensaries) without patent holder's consent.

Section 92 allows compulsory licensing by notification during national emergency, extreme urgency, or public non-commercial use. No need to wait 3 years from grant. COVID-19 example: government can authorize manufacture of any patented drug/vaccine under Section 92 notification. TRIPS Article 31bis allows export of compulsory-licensed medicines to countries without manufacturing capacity. For AYUSH: during health emergencies, patented AYUSH medicines could be compulsorily licensed for public health response.

Section 92A allows compulsory license for manufacture and export of patented pharmaceutical products to countries with insufficient manufacturing capacity facing public health emergencies. Implements TRIPS Article 31bis (Doha Declaration). Requirements: importing country has granted compulsory license or allowed importation, product for addressing public health problem, quantity limited to importing country's needs. For Indian AYUSH manufacturers: can potentially export compulsory-licensed AYUSH medicines to developing countries facing health crises, if such license is granted.

Procedure for compulsory license under Section 84: 1) File application with Controller (Form 17) with evidence supporting grounds. 2) Pay fee (Rs 2,000). 3) Controller notifies patent holder. 4) Patent holder can file opposition within prescribed time. 5) Hearing before Controller. 6) Controller decides — can grant license with terms including royalty rate, territory, duration, scope. 7) Appeal to Appellate Board/High Court. Typical royalty: 4-7% of net sales (Natco case: 6%). Timeline: 6-12 months typically.

What is 'reasonably affordable price'? No fixed formula, but factors considered: 1) Price in India vs other countries. 2) R&D costs and recoupment. 3) Purchasing power of Indian consumers. 4) Price of comparable products. 5) Public health importance. 6) Patent holder's profit margins. In Natco case, patentee's price was Rs 2.8 lakh/month; compulsory licensee priced at Rs 8,800/month. For AYUSH: if patented formulation priced significantly higher than comparable non-patented alternatives, may trigger compulsory license application.

Section 83 declares that patents are granted to encourage inventions and secure that they are WORKED in India. 'Worked' means manufactured to a reasonable extent or adequately imported. Key principle: patents should benefit Indian industry and consumers, not just be blocking rights. Form 27 (annual working statement) enforces this. Non-working for 3+ years can lead to: compulsory licensing, revocation proceedings. For AYUSH patentees: set up manufacturing in India or license to Indian manufacturers to avoid compulsory licensing risk.

Section 91 covers compulsory licenses for dependent patents: if a later patent cannot be worked without infringing an earlier patent, and the later patent involves important technical advance of economic significance, the later patentee can seek compulsory license on the earlier patent. Cross-license may be required. For AYUSH: if your improved formulation (patented) uses a technique patented by someone else, you may need to seek compulsory license or negotiate cross-license to commercialize.

Section 85 allows revocation of patent if, even after compulsory license is granted, reasonable public requirements are not satisfied, or invention is not available at reasonable price. This is the ultimate sanction for non-working. Process: application to Controller, hearing, revocation order. Rarely used but available as a tool. For AYUSH patentees: ensure genuine commercialization efforts; mere licensing without actual production may not suffice.

Section 86 allows Controller to endorse patent as 'license of right' after 3 years from grant if public requirements not satisfied but circumstances don't warrant full compulsory license. Effect: any person can obtain license on terms settled by Controller. Patent holder cannot refuse. Useful for encouraging broader manufacturing while maintaining some patent value. For AYUSH: license of right can enable multiple manufacturers to produce patented formulation, increasing availability and competition.

Several AYUSH formulations may qualify as 'essential medicines' for public health. National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) currently focuses on allopathic drugs but AYUSH Ministry promotes integration. If AYUSH medicines are added to essential lists, compulsory licensing provisions become more relevant. AYUSH Ministry's initiative for 'Essential AYUSH Medicines' for Primary Health Centres: creates potential for government use provisions. Patentees should consider pricing and availability strategies to avoid compulsory licensing risk.
